summary: Describes how XMPP addresses and messages map to the Common Presence and Instant Messaging (CPIM) specifications. This lets XMPP systems exchange messages and presence with other systems that speak CPIM.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a translation guide between two chat languages so that people on different chat systems can still talk to each other.

questions: xmpp interoperability with other im systems
how does xmpp map to cpim
what is an xmpp cpim gateway
how is xmpp presence mapped to pidf
subtitle: A translation table that lets an XMPP chat service exchange messages and presence with other instant messaging systems.

tldr.problem: XMPP and the CPIM family of instant messaging specifications use different address formats and message syntaxes, so an XMPP service cannot directly talk to a non-XMPP service that follows CPIM.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how XMPP addresses, message stanzas and presence stanzas map to CPIM addresses, Message/CPIM headers and PIDF presence documents, and back, for use in an XMPP-CPIM gateway.
tldr.outcome: A gateway can translate the core parts of messages and presence in both directions. Extra XMPP and CPIM features that have no counterpart are mostly dropped.

today: RFC 3922 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the XMPP specifications in RFC 3920 and RFC 3921 and pairs with RFC 3923 for secured traffic.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The IMPP Working Group defined an abstract framework for interoperability among instant messaging (IM) and presence systems, commonly called CPIM (Common Presence and Instant Messaging). It includes a Common Profile for Instant Messaging, a Common Profile for Presence, a CPIM Message Format and a Presence Information Data Format (PIDF).

RFC 3922 describes how XMPP (RFC 3920, RFC 3921) maps onto that abstract model, mainly so that someone can build an XMPP-CPIM gateway between an XMPP service and a non-XMPP service. The gateway is not an intermediate hop between non-XMPP servers. It is a dedicated translator, and the CPIM formats are the common ground it translates into.

The mapping covers messages and presence that are not encrypted or signed end to end. Secured traffic is handled by RFC 3923.
sections.plainLanguage: Two chat apps speak different languages. This document is the dictionary for a translator who sits between them.

sections.title: The Approach
sections.content:
The RFC calls XMPP and CPIM distinctly foreign technologies. XMPP streams XML elements called stanzas between endpoints and is not based on MIME. CPIM instead uses two MIME content types: Message/CPIM for messages and application/pidf+xml for presence.

So the approach is to map XMPP elements and attributes to the headers and MIME formats of the CPIM message format and PIDF, and to define the reverse mappings too. Messages travel as a Message/CPIM object that carries text content. Presence travels as a Message/CPIM object that carries an encapsulated PIDF document.
sections.plainLanguage: One chat system sends little XML notes. The other puts notes in labelled envelopes. The translator moves each note into the right kind of envelope.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content:
XMPP addresses differ from the im: URIs used for instant inboxes and the pres: URIs used for presentities. The characters &, ' and / are allowed in im: and pres: URIs but not in XMPP addresses, and many non-ASCII UTF-8 characters are allowed in XMPP local parts but not in those URIs. Only local parts are covered. Domain name mapping is out of scope.

To go from XMPP to CPIM, split the address into node, domain and resource, and discard the resource. Optionally apply the Nodeprep profile of stringprep. Translate the escape sequences for &, ' and /. Percent-encode every byte outside the set A-Za-z0-9!$*.?_~+=. Recombine with the mapped host and prepend im: for message stanzas or pres: for presence stanzas.

The reverse direction removes the scheme, splits at the first @, decodes percent-escapes, treats the result as UTF-8, reverses the character translations, optionally applies Nodeprep, and recombines the parts.
sections.plainLanguage: Each system writes street addresses differently. The translator rewrites every address in the other system's style and swaps out any characters the other side does not allow.

sections.title: Mapping Instant Messages
sections.content:
A gateway SHOULD map messages using a Message/CPIM object that wraps text content. Because XMPP uses UTF-8 exclusively, the encapsulated content MUST be text/plain with the charset set to utf-8.

From XMPP to CPIM, the from and to attributes become the From and To headers. The gateway MUST remove the resource identifier, MUST prepend im: and MAY add a Formal-name. The <subject/> element becomes the Subject header, with xml:lang carried as ;lang=tag. The <body/> text becomes the encapsulated content. The stanza type and the <thread/> element have no mapping and SHOULD be ignored. The id attribute SHOULD NOT be mapped to the MIME Content-ID unless it is known to be unique. Extension content SHOULD be ignored, except content in the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-e2e namespace.

From CPIM to XMPP, the gateway strips the im: scheme and any Formal-name, and maps Subject and text/plain content back. The cc and DateTime headers SHOULD NOT be passed on, and NS headers MUST NOT be. A Require header cannot be honoured without knowing the receiver, so the gateway SHOULD return a warning or error to the sender. Content that is not text/plain MUST NOT go into <body/>. The gateway MUST map the message if the charset is US-ASCII or UTF-8, and otherwise SHOULD NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender, receiver, subject and message text get copied into the new envelope. Anything the other system has no slot for, like a conversation thread, is left behind.

sections.title: Mapping Presence Information
sections.content:
Presence uses a Message/CPIM object that carries an application/pidf+xml document, with charset utf-8. The XMPP from address maps to the CPIM From header and also to the PIDF entity attribute (with a pres: scheme). The gateway SHOULD map the resource identifier to the id of the PIDF <tuple/>.

A presence stanza with no type means available and maps to the PIDF basic status OPEN. A type of unavailable maps to CLOSED. The XMPP <show/> values (away, chat, dnd, xa) are meant to map to extended status in the PIDF IM namespace once values are defined. The <status/> text maps to the PIDF <note/>.

XMPP priority is an integer from -128 to +127. A gateway MAY map it to the PIDF priority attribute, a number from zero to one with at most three decimals. Negative values MUST NOT be mapped. The RFC suggests 0 maps to 0 and 127 to 1, and calls its intermediate values an example only.

In the other direction, a gateway MAY include the complete PIDF document as a child of the presence stanza for clients that can parse it. A PIDF document with several tuples is split into several XMPP presence stanzas.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence is like a sign on your door that says in or out, plus a note. The translator copies the sign and the note onto the other system's door sign.

sections.title: The Gateway as a Presence Service
sections.content:
A gateway MAY act as a presence service, so that XMPP users can subscribe to non-XMPP presentities and the reverse. The RFC defines only the XMPP side of these interactions, because PIDF has no syntax for operations such as subscribe.

To subscribe, an XMPP entity sends a presence stanza of type subscribe. Its from maps to the CPP watcher parameter and its to to the target parameter, both with the pres: scheme. There is no mapping for the duration parameter, since XMPP subscriptions last until explicitly cancelled. If approved, the gateway MUST return subscribed and the current presence, then notify on every change. If denied, it MUST return unsubscribed. The errors are <item-not-found/>, <forbidden/> and, as a SHOULD, <conflict/>.

Unsubscribing uses type unsubscribe, and cancelling someone else's subscription uses unsubscribed. Both set the duration parameter to zero and stop further notifications. The gateway MUST NOT generate a PIDF document with zero tuples from an XMPP presence stanza.
sections.plainLanguage: Subscribing is asking a friend to tell you whenever they come online. The translator passes the request along, relays the yes or no, and keeps passing on updates until someone says stop.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the IM and presence requirements in RFC 2779 for detailed security considerations. A gateway MUST be compliant with the minimum security requirements of the instant messaging and presence protocols it interfaces with.

Gateways add new risks. End-to-end confidentiality and integrity between user agents on either side of a gateway can be provided only if both sides support common formats, which RFC 3923 specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator in the middle could peek at or change notes. To stay safe, both sides need to seal their notes in a way the translator passes through untouched.
